title: Brazil’s real sinks after Lula’s re-election victory
author: Al Jazeera Staff
text: SaveSharefacebookxwhatsapp-strokecopylinkBrazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's election win has triggered financial uncertainty as right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede [Juan Barreto/AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 26 Oct 202626 Oct 2026Brazil’s real dropped against the United States dollar on the heels of Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s unexpected re-election after right-wing Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, led in the first round of voting earlier this month.Brazil’s currency dropped against the dollar by 12 percent in spot trading. Bovespa stock index futures tumbled nearly 15 percent on Monday.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3World reacts to Lula’s victory in Brazil’s presidential electionlist 2 of 3Lula’s victory may be a turning point for Latin Americalist 3 of 3How did Lula beat Bolsonaro after losing Brazil’s first-round election?end of list“I’m not surprised the real is sinking sharply; traders are covering their bets that assume a Bolsonaro victory and tighter fiscal policy,” Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.Brazil’s stock exchange halted trading for 30 minutes. The Bovespa index fell 10 percent from its previous close, triggering a circuit-breaker safety mechanism and reversing a rally earlier this month amid expectations of a shift to the right after Bolsonaro won the first round.Ziemba says Bolsonaro’s refusal to concede the election has driven some financial uncertainty.“The market pressure is also amplified by the objections raised by Bolsonaro, but the scale of the victory suggests that the result will stand,” she said.Interest rate futures had also reflected expectations that tighter fiscal policy under Bolsonaro would allow borrowing costs to decline.“They [investors] assume more domestic spending and higher rates in Brazil. However, the real is still likely to be supported by strong commodity revenues,” Ziemba noted.Stocks closed on Friday almost 7 percent above their level before the first round, while the Brazilian real was nearly 5 percent stronger against the US dollar. Advertisement Interest rate futures are up 3.1 percent, rising sharply after President Lula’s win. Interest rate futures had previously reflected a tighter fiscal policy amid expectations that Bolsonaro would oust the incumbent and that he would allow borrowing costs to decline.Sign up for Al JazeeraAmericas Coverage Newsletterprotected by reCAPTCHALula faces an increase in Brazil’s debt and will be challenged with protecting both social programmes and investment, with investors looking for signs of whether his gradual fiscal approach can bring borrowing costs down.Lula’s team aims to produce a budget surplus of about 1.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030. That would leave money to cover part of the interest bill, reducing the need for fresh borrowing. But public debt already exceeds 82 percent of GDP, while pensions and other legally required spending limit where savings can come from.“Lula’s policies have talked about spending cuts, but he has not gone into the details of how that is going to look,” said Divya Singaravelu, head of research at Meridian 1305 Capital.Attention will now turn to Lula’s choice of finance minister and what it signals about his fiscal approach.
